questions.stem: By which process does water enter a root hair cell?

options.explanation: Condensation is a gas-to-liquid change, not cell uptake.

options.text: Osmosis, down a water potential gradient
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Evaporation belongs to the leaf surface, not the root.
That is a white cell feeding mechanism, not plant uptake.

questions.stem: How do root hair cells take in mineral ions?

options.explanation: Nothing evaporates at the root hair surface.
Uptake often runs against the gradient, so energy is required.

options.text: By active transport, powered by energy from mitochondria
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: By osmosis along with the water
options.explanation: Ions are not water; osmosis moves water only.

questions.stem: Why does a root hair cell contain many mitochondria?

options.explanation: Water is not stored in mitochondria.
Roots are dark; photosynthesis cannot run there.

options.text: To make the cell wall thicker
options.explanation: Walls are built from other materials, not mitochondrial work.

options.text: To release the energy that active transport of ions demands
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

questions.stem: Which advantage do the hair-like extensions give the root?

options.text: A greatly increased surface area for faster uptake
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: A shorter route to the leaves
options.explanation: The route upward runs through the xylem, unchanged.
These are underground cells; wind is irrelevant.
Storage is a cortex or seed role, not the hair's job.

questions.stem: State the two transport processes a root hair cell uses and what each moves.
questions.modelAnswer: Osmosis moves water in, and active transport moves mineral ions in.

questions.stem: Name the organelle that powers ion uptake in root hair cells.
questions.modelAnswer: Mitochondria release the energy used for active transport.

questions.stem: Explain why the shape of a root hair cell suits its absorbing role.
questions.modelAnswer: The long, thin extension multiplies the surface area in contact with soil water, so osmosis and active transport can proceed at a much higher rate.

questions.stem: A seedling is transplanted with most root hairs broken off. Predict the effect and explain it.
questions.modelAnswer: Water and ion uptake drops sharply, because the absorbing surface area has been lost, so the seedling wilts until new hairs grow.

questions.stem: Which sequence gives the correct pathway of water across a root?

options.text: Cortex cells, root hair cell, xylem
options.explanation: The hair cell is the first stop, not the second.

options.text: Root hair cell, root cortex cells, xylem
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Xylem, cortex cells, root hair cell
options.explanation: That runs backwards; uptake starts at the surface.

options.text: Root hair cell, xylem, cortex cells
options.explanation: The cortex sits between the hair and the xylem.

questions.stem: Water moves from the xylem into which leaf cells at the end of its journey?

options.explanation: The epidermis is the leaf's outer skin, not the endpoint of supply.
Phloem carries sugars, not the incoming water supply.
Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Guard cells adjust stomata; the main destination is the mesophyll.

questions.stem: What decides the direction water moves at each step across the root?

options.text: The sugar concentration of the xylem
options.explanation: Sugar is the phloem's cargo, not the water driver.
Mitochondria matter for ion pumps, not osmosis.
Colour has no role in water movement.

questions.stem: Which process moves water between the cortex cells?

questions.stem: Why does the soil usually supply water to the root rather than the reverse?

options.text: Because gravity holds water in the soil
options.explanation: Gravity acts on drainage, not on cell-level osmosis.

options.text: Soil water potential is higher than the root cell's, so osmosis points inward
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: Because the root pushes water outward at night
options.explanation: No outward push exists.
Saltier means lower potential, which would reverse the flow.

questions.stem: Write out the pathway of water through the plant in order.
questions.modelAnswer: From the root hair cell across the cortex into the xylem and finally the leaf's mesophyll.

questions.stem: Define water potential in simple terms.
questions.modelAnswer: It measures how freely water molecules can move in a solution.

questions.stem: Explain why water keeps flowing inward even after the root hair cells are saturated.
questions.modelAnswer: Because the xylem and the leaf beyond it maintain a lower water potential, so the gradient never disappears and osmosis continues inward.

questions.stem: Seawater splashes onto a coastal plant's soil. Predict what happens to water uptake and justify it.
questions.modelAnswer: Uptake falls or reverses, because the salt lowers the soil's water potential below that of the root cells, so osmosis no longer points inward.
